section_summary: This section documents requests from American legislators, travelers, and intermediaries for admission to Japanese imperial garden parties, palace visits, and imperial audiences between 1932 and 1937. State Department and Embassy officials explain that invitations to the spring Cherry Blossom and autumn Chrysanthemum parties were tightly controlled by Japanese authorities, while visits to the Kyoto Imperial Palace could be arranged through the American Embassy. The section also covers restrictions on consular invitations, proposed ceremonies for a visiting congressional delegation, and the refusal to seek an imperial audience for journalist Rudolph Block.

subfiles.title: Request for Eliza M. Carr Flowers to attend the Imperial Chrysanthemum Party
subfiles.about: Morrison asks the State Department to recommend Eliza M. Carr Flowers for the November 8 Imperial Chrysanthemum Party.
subfiles.summary: Morrison describes Flowers as a charming member of a prominent North Carolina family and supplies her Yokohama address. The second page is an associated State Department routing or cover sheet with little legible substantive text.

subfiles.title: Reply directing Flowers to Ambassador Grew
subfiles.about: The Department explains that requests for invitations to foreign functions are left to the discretion of the American mission concerned.
subfiles.summary: The reply declines to make the requested recommendation directly. It suggests that Flowers communicate with Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo for advice.

subfiles.title: Transmission of A. H. Carr's request for Flowers
subfiles.about: Morrison forwards A. H. Carr's letter and again requests permission for Flowers to attend the November 8 party.
subfiles.summary: The senator asks for early advice and for the enclosure to be returned to his files. The request concerns the annual Imperial Chrysanthemum Party at Shinjuku Imperial Garden.

subfiles.title: A. H. Carr's appeal on behalf of his sister
subfiles.about: Carr asks Morrison to obtain a State Department recommendation for Carr's sister to attend the Imperial Chrysanthemum Party.
subfiles.summary: Carr says his sister is already in Japan and believes Americans must be recommended by the Department. He acknowledges that little time remains and gives her address in care of Thomas Cook and Son at Yokohama.

subfiles.title: Return of Carr enclosure to Senator Morrison
subfiles.about: Stimson returns the enclosure accompanying Morrison's second letter concerning Flowers.
subfiles.summary: The letter refers to Morrison's communications of October 20 and October 25 about the Imperial Chrysanthemum Party. It returns A. H. Carr's letter as requested without offering a new decision.

subfiles.title: Bailey request for Flowers to attend the Cherry Blossom Festival
subfiles.about: Bailey asks Stimson to recommend Flowers for the following spring's imperial Cherry Blossom Festival.
subfiles.summary: Bailey identifies Flowers as the daughter of General Julian S. Carr and praises her character. He says Americans apparently must be recommended by the State Department and supplies her Yokohama address.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning the Cherry Blossom Festival
subfiles.about: The Department tells Bailey that garden-party invitations are outside both its jurisdiction and that of the ambassador.
subfiles.summary: The reply declines to procure an invitation for Flowers. It nevertheless suggests contacting Ambassador Grew, who may be able to provide further details.

subfiles.title: Bailey's renewed request for an imperial garden-party invitation
subfiles.about: Bailey renews his request after hearing that the State Department, rather than the Embassy, designates prospective garden-party invitees.
subfiles.summary: Bailey quotes instructions reportedly received by Flowers and asks the Department to designate her to the Embassy. He again invokes her family background and gives her Yokohama address.

subfiles.title: Reply to Bailey's renewed request
subfiles.about: The Department reiterates that neither it nor Ambassador Grew controls invitations to Imperial Garden Parties.
subfiles.summary: The reply refers Bailey to the Department's December 16 explanation and notes that Grew can provide information but may not take affirmative action. Copies of the correspondence will nonetheless be sent to Grew so that he has the relevant background.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Grew about handling garden-party applications
subfiles.from: James Grafton Rogers, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department sends Bailey's correspondence to Grew and requests a statement of the Embassy's procedure for garden-party applications.
subfiles.summary: The Department expects no further action on Flowers's personal request but wants to prevent misunderstandings in future cases. It asks Grew to confirm whether the Embassy gives applicants a uniform reply and encloses both exchanges with Bailey.

subfiles.title: File memorandum identifying Grew's response
subfiles.about: The memorandum notes that Tokyo despatch No. 352 states the Embassy's standard response to garden-party requests.
subfiles.summary: The brief filing note links the Department's inquiry to Grew's March 22 despatch. It indicates that the despatch supplies the requested policy statement.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch on applications for Imperial Garden Parties
subfiles.about: Grew reports the standard Embassy response to people seeking invitations to Imperial Garden Parties.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy tells applicants that regulations changed after an October 15, 1926 notice from the Japanese Foreign Office. Invitations are now limited to government officials in Tokyo or high officials passing through Japan whose attendance the Foreign Office desires; page 17 is an associated departmental filing sheet.

subfiles.title: Despatch protesting restrictions on consular invitations
subfiles.about: Garrels reports a new alternating-year system for inviting Tokyo and Yokohama consuls to imperial garden parties.
subfiles.summary: Garrels accepts the imperial household's right to select guests but considers the discrimination against approximately thirty career and honorary consular officers difficult to justify. He argues that consular officers normally receive ceremonial precedence and notes that his British colleague did not acknowledge the restriction.

subfiles.title: Tokyo governor's notice restricting consular invitations
subfiles.about: Kosaka announces that Tokyo and Yokohama consuls will henceforth receive invitations in alternating years.
subfiles.summary: The notice attributes the restriction to the growing number of guests at the Cherry Blossom and Chrysanthemum parties. It gives a schedule alternating the two cities between the spring and autumn events beginning in 1933.

subfiles.title: Kiplinger request for assistance to the Dentons
subfiles.about: Kiplinger asks Hornbeck to help Albert H. Denton and his wife attend a November chrysanthemum display.
subfiles.summary: The Dentons believe admission to the Yokohama event requires an invitation from Ambassador Grew. Kiplinger recommends Denton as a leading Arkansas City banker and former member of the United States Shipping Board.

subfiles.title: Appointment note concerning Fujii
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs staff
subfiles.about: The note records Fujii's scheduled calls on the under secretary and Hornbeck.
subfiles.summary: Fujii is expected to see the under secretary at 11:30 a.m. and Hornbeck at noon on Friday. The note prepares for the possible use of that meeting in the Denton matter.

subfiles.title: Suggestion to ask Fujii about the Dentons
subfiles.about: An internal memorandum suggests asking Fujii to arrange the Dentons' attendance through the Imperial Household Department.
subfiles.summary: Fujii is expected to call on William Phillips about the Japanese shipping tax case and then visit Hornbeck. The writer believes Fujii would willingly raise the Dentons' garden-party request with the appropriate Japanese authorities.

subfiles.title: Explanation of chrysanthemum exhibitions and invitation policy
subfiles.about: Hornbeck distinguishes the invitation-only Imperial Garden Party from public and private chrysanthemum exhibitions.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck explains that foreign diplomats lost their power to nominate guests to imperial parties in 1926 and that the Embassy now requests invitations only for qualifying American officials. He adds that Ambassador Grew and his staff should be able to help the Dentons find the best publicly accessible displays.

subfiles.title: Letter introducing the Denton request to Ambassador Grew
subfiles.about: Hornbeck forwards the Kiplinger correspondence and asks Grew to assist the Dentons where appropriate.
subfiles.summary: Copies of Kiplinger's October 2 letter and Hornbeck's October 4 reply are enclosed. Hornbeck expresses confidence that Grew will enjoy meeting the Dentons and give them suitable assistance.

subfiles.title: Kiplinger acknowledgment of Hornbeck's assistance
subfiles.about: Kiplinger thanks Hornbeck and clarifies that he merely wanted Grew to know the Dentons were not ordinary tourists.
subfiles.summary: Kiplinger says he did not intend to burden Hornbeck with the chrysanthemum matter. His purpose was to have the letter forwarded to his acquaintance Joe Grew as a personal introduction.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note for Neville's congressional-delegation telegram
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a telegram about Japanese wishes for a longer congressional visit and an imperial audience.
subfiles.summary: It records Japanese interest in having the vice president and congressional party spend more time in Japan after Manila. It also notes that the women in the party would not be presented because the empress was not granting audiences that year.

subfiles.title: Telegram on a possible imperial audience for the congressional party
subfiles.about: Neville reports Japanese inquiries about the composition of a possible imperial audience for the vice president's party.
subfiles.summary: Neville proposes that the vice president might be accompanied by the House speaker, committee chairmen, and congressional floor leaders, while acknowledging that court etiquette and room size prevent reception of the entire party. Japanese officials also hope the delegation will make a longer return visit after Manila, and press comment has been favorable.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on proposed Tokyo state dinner
subfiles.about: The note concerns a proposed October 25 state dinner in Tokyo honoring Vice President Garner.
subfiles.summary: Walsh records consultation with Hawes about whether such a dinner should be held. Hawes opposes it because he lacks authority to keep the congressional party overnight in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Maverick transmission of Frost's palace request
subfiles.about: Maverick forwards a constituent's request for permission to visit an imperial palace in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Maverick describes the correspondent as a highly regarded San Antonio resident. He asks Hull to refer the request to the proper office and provide instructions that can be relayed to Jonas M. Frost.

subfiles.title: Frost request for Imperial Palace access
subfiles.about: Frost asks Maverick to obtain permission for two families to visit an imperial palace during a summer trip to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Frost believes the Japanese government may issue permission when requested by an American consul. He says the Frost and Marko families will form a party of seven and asks whether access can be arranged through the Japanese ambassador or the State Department.

subfiles.title: Telephone memorandum listing the Frost-Marko party
subfiles.about: The memorandum records the names and citizenship status of the Frost and Marko travelers.
subfiles.summary: Maverick's secretary supplies the names of Jonas and Pearl Frost, Isadore and Rebecca Marko, and the Marko children Joseph and Irma Carlyne. Maverick requests immediate letters and vouches for each traveler's American citizenship.

subfiles.title: Passport Division query about answering Maverick
subfiles.about: A Passport Division official asks whether the division should answer Maverick's communication.
subfiles.summary: The writer notes that Mr. Duvall of the Far Eastern Affairs division left the file in Shipley's office. Because the division cannot yet identify passport applications for both families, the writer suggests waiting for passports before issuing introduction letters.

subfiles.title: Passport Division memorandum on responsibility for the reply
subfiles.about: The memorandum advises that Passport Division should not answer Maverick directly.
subfiles.summary: The writer considers a direct Passport Division response inappropriate. Instead, the division should furnish Far Eastern Affairs with a paragraph concerning the requested letters of introduction.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs guidance on visiting the Kyoto Palace
subfiles.about: The division supplies language explaining the procedure for obtaining permission to visit the Kyoto Imperial Palace.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum concludes that Frost probably means Kyoto rather than Tokyo, because the Tokyo Imperial Palace is never open to the public. It states that Kyoto permits can normally be secured within two days through the American Embassy after an informal application naming all visitors.

subfiles.title: Passport Division routing note for the Frost-Marko case
subfiles.about: The fragmentary note routes or indexes the congressional correspondence concerning the Frost and Marko names.
subfiles.summary: Only brief references to Maverick, Frost, and Marko remain legible. The page appears to be an internal Passport Division filing or routing slip associated with the palace-access request.

subfiles.title: Reply to Maverick with palace-visit instructions
subfiles.about: Shipley sends introduction letters and explains how the travelers may obtain permission to visit the Kyoto Imperial Palace.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy in Tokyo can usually obtain Kyoto permits within two days after receiving the visitors' names by telephone or letter. Shipley emphasizes that the Tokyo Imperial Palace is never open to the public and encloses two introduction letters plus Frost's original letter.

subfiles.title: Letter of introduction for the Frost family
subfiles.about: Hull introduces Jonas M. Frost, his wife Pearl, and their son for their trip abroad.
subfiles.summary: The letter is issued at Representative Maverick's request, with Maverick vouching for the family's citizenship. Hull asks American officers to extend courtesies and assistance consistent with their duties.

subfiles.title: Letter of introduction for the Marko family
subfiles.about: Hull introduces Isadore and Rebecca Marko and their children Irma Carlyne and Joseph for travel abroad.
subfiles.summary: The letter is prepared at Representative Maverick's request, and he vouches for the family's citizenship. Hull asks diplomatic and consular officers to offer appropriate courtesies and assistance.

subfiles.title: Sanford request for Kyoto Imperial Palace access
subfiles.about: Sanford asks how he, his wife, and Mrs. A. P. Lockett may obtain permission to enter the Kyoto Imperial Palace.
subfiles.summary: Sanford expects to visit Japan in September and has read that tourists require a request from consular or embassy sources. He asks for assistance only if it follows normal procedure and creates no inconvenience for Hull.

subfiles.title: Reply explaining the Kyoto Palace permit procedure
subfiles.about: McBride advises Sanford to apply through the American Embassy after arriving in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Permits can reportedly be obtained on short notice through an informal application by telephone. Sanford should provide every visitor's name and an address where the permits can be delivered.

subfiles.title: Memorandum approving Grew's refusal to seek an audience for Bruno Lessing
subfiles.about: The memorandum endorses Grew's decision not to seek an imperial audience for journalist Rudolph Block, who wrote as Bruno Lessing.
subfiles.summary: After consulting the Japanese Foreign Office, Grew judged that Block lacked sufficient prominence in journalism to qualify. The memorandum notes that imperial rules limited such applications to high government officials, people of high social position, or persons with worldwide reputations in recognized fields.
